Lock projects behind your approval

peer_auth - the daemon in its own OS account, a Unix socket that names each caller by its uid, and locked projects your own agents reach only with an approval you prove.

On this page

  • Lock from the console, or force lock in the file

  • Deploy it: the daemon runs as its own account

  • Enroll an approver

  • Requests
  • Approve: three paths, one core
  • Leases and the process tree

  • Restricted local accounts

  • Updates

Project isolation keeps agents working on one project out of another's knowledge. It is a policy fence: it trusts the session binding an agent reports, every caller shares one bearer key, and the corpus is files in your home directory that any process of yours can read.

peer_auth is the boundary underneath it, for when the threat is your own account: an agent of yours reading a project it should not, through Seamless or through a file. One daemon serves everyone, running as an OS account of its own. It identifies each caller by the uid the kernel reports for its Unix-socket connection, never by anything the caller sends.

On that boundary you can lock a project. A locked project stays closed to every agent of yours until you approve one agent's access, for a limited time, with a proof the agent cannot produce: Touch ID, a passkey, or your own sudo. The approval covers that agent and the programs it started, and nothing else.

It is off by default, and off means exactly the behavior every release before it had. It asks for a different deployment (the daemon needs an account of its own, or the files would not hold), and it runs on macOS and Linux only: Windows has no Unix-socket peer credentials Seamless can read.

Two settings: isolation and the lock

Isolation says what flows in and out of a project. The lock says whether even its own agents need a fresh approval from you before reaching it. They are two settings, with two words: "sealed" is an isolation state, and the lock is never called that.

Isolation The lock
Question What flows in and out of this project? Must even this project's own agents get your approval first?
Values open, confidential, sealed locked or not
Set on the console's project Overview, or with seam project isolation on the console's project Overview with a passkey, or forced in the daemon's config file
Needs peer_auth no yes
  • confidential is for sensitive work your agents should still do freely: nothing leaves the project, and its sessions still read open projects and the global scope. It needs no extra deployment.
  • sealed is a clean room: nothing in or out.
  • Locked is for what no agent should touch without you saying so now: money, legal matters, credentials. Reaching one takes your approval, session by session.

Sensitive projects are normally confidential and locked: once you approve an agent, its session still reads your open projects and the global scope. serve refuses a locked project that is open, because the isolation fence is what keeps it out of the family, parent and cross-project gardener surfaces the lock does not reach on its own.

Lock from the console, or force lock in the file

There are two ways to lock a project, and they differ in who can undo them.

From the console. On a confidential or sealed project, open the Isolation card on its Overview and choose Lock this project. The change needs a passkey you have already enrolled; until you have one, the card links to the Approvers page instead. Taking the lock off takes a passkey too, from the same page or the project's unlock page. Each approval names one project and one direction, so it cannot be replayed for anything else. Turning a lock on ends every approval the project still had (agents' leases, read grants and browser unlocks), so each agent and browser asks again. Seamless applies the change by restarting, which briefly drops the console and agent connections.

Force lock, in the file. A project listed under peer_auth.force_locked is force locked: the console shows it as force locked and cannot change it, even with a passkey. Only editing the file and restarting removes it. Use this for a project that should stay locked however the console is reached.

The console removes only the locks it set. A project in both places stays locked until it leaves the file. While a project is locked, by either route, its isolation cannot be set to open: remove the lock first.

Console lock changes are passkey-only for now. A Touch ID key enrolled with seam touchid enroll approves agents' requests but cannot approve these; a passkey saved on your Mac still asks for your fingerprint in the browser.

The key was called peer_auth.locked in earlier builds. That name still works, and seamlessd doctor warns until you rename it.

How it decides

Every request carries a principal, set by the transport before any route runs:

Connection Principal
TCP with the bearer key the owner account (peer_auth.owner)
The socket, from the owner's uid the owner, with its kernel-reported process chain
The socket, from a uid listed under peer_auth.restricted that restricted account
The socket, from any other uid refused with 403 before any route runs

For the owner, the rule is simple. Every project that is not locked behaves exactly as it does without peer_auth, isolation fences included. A locked project is closed to every owner request: its name, description, isolation and item counts show, nothing inside it does, and writes into it are refused, unless the request rides a socket connection whose process holds a live lease. A TCP request never holds one, because a shared key cannot be tied to one process.

"Closed" means every surface: recall, briefings, the prompt matcher, every MCP tool by name or by id, tasks, trials, sessions, the gardener's proposals, the hooks, A2A, the console and its live feed. A call that names a locked project is refused with the rule and the remedy, never with any of its content. A recall that names no project answers from the rest of its scope and says <project> (locked) may hold results; project_list lists the project with the way in.

Configure it

peer_auth:
  enabled: true
  owner: alice                      # the account the TCP bearer key stands for
  socket:
    path: /opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock
    mode: "0666"                    # who may knock; the kernel still names each one
  force_locked: [example-finance]   # only this file can remove these; each must be confidential or sealed
  max_lease: 8h                     # optional: caps every approval, at most 24h

Every key is in the configuration reference.

Checked when the file loads, whether or not enabled is set: force_locked names real projects, never the global scope, and none twice; restricted is listed only with enabled set, and never names the owner or the same account twice; max_lease and passkeys are well formed. With enabled set, also: the owner is named, the socket path is absolute and outside data_dir, and the mode is octal and keeps owner read and write.

Checked when serve starts, and refused if any fails:

  • every account resolves on this machine (macOS role accounts live in the directory service, and are found there), and no two entries share a uid;
  • every project the block names exists - a misspelled lock would leave the project it meant open, which is exactly what this feature exists to prevent;
  • every locked project is confidential or sealed;
  • the files would hold too (the next section).

seamlessd doctor, run as the daemon's account against the daemon's config, prints the policy as it resolved and every reason serve would refuse.

Coming from peer_auth.users. A config with a non-empty users map is refused when it loads, even while peer_auth is disabled, with:

config: peer_auth.users was the 2026-10-31 design, which sealed projects to other OS accounts, and is no longer supported: list the projects under peer_auth.force_locked and remove users

That map reserved projects for other OS accounts, and you could never reach them. It is gone. List those projects under peer_auth.force_locked, keep each one confidential or sealed, delete users, and restart. An account that was listed there is then refused at the socket unless you list it under peer_auth.restricted, which reaches only open projects that are not locked.

Deploy it: the daemon runs as its own account

The data directory holds every project's memory in plain files and a SQLite database. If the daemon runs as you, every process of yours reads them. So with peer_auth on, serve refuses to start unless:

  • it runs as neither the owner nor root, and as the account the pin below names (with no pin, as a system account);
  • data_dir belongs to the daemon's account and is mode 0700;
  • the socket's directory belongs to the daemon's account or root and is not group- or world-writable (whoever can write it can replace the socket and impersonate the daemon to every caller);
  • every directory above the data, the socket, the config file and the binary belongs to root or the daemon's account and is not writable by anyone else - a directory you own anywhere above the data is one you can rename it out of;
  • the config file and the seamlessd binary belong to root or the daemon's account and are not group- or world-writable: whoever can rewrite either can switch the boundary off at the next start;
  • with TLS on, tls.cert_file and tls.key_file are held to the same rule, and no other account can read the key (its group may, only when that group is the daemon's own): whoever reads the key can serve the daemon's own name with its certificate, on another port or address.

A layout that satisfies all of it:

Path Owner Mode Holds
/opt/seamless root 0755
/opt/seamless/bin root 0755 seamlessd, seam (both 0755, root's)
/opt/seamless/etc root 0755 seamless.yaml (root:_seamless, 0640), daemon-account (root's, 0644)
/opt/seamless/etc/tls root:_seamless 0750 with TLS on: the certificate (0644) and its key (root:_seamless, 0640)
/opt/seamless/data _seamless 0700 the database and corpus
/opt/seamless/run _seamless 0755 the socket
/opt/seamless/home _seamless 0700 the account's home (caches, nothing else)

A daemon that updates itself holds /opt/seamless/bin and both binaries as _seamless instead of root, still 0755: your account can write neither way.

Create the account as a system account: on macOS a uid below 500, on Linux one below UID_MIN in /etc/login.defs (1000 unless the file says otherwise). The commands below make one. Until the account is pinned (after the layout), seam approve, seam touchid enroll, the Touch ID approver and serve accept any system account as the daemon's, and no other.

On macOS, as an administrator, pick an unused uid in the role range, below 500 (dscl . -list /Users UniqueID lists the taken ones):

sudo dscl . -create /Groups/_seamless PrimaryGroupID 480
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless UniqueID 480
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless PrimaryGroupID 480
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless UserShell /usr/bin/false
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless NFSHomeDirectory /opt/seamless/home
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless Password '*'
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless IsHidden 1

On Linux:

sudo useradd --system --user-group --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --home-dir /opt/seamless/home _seamless

Then the layout (root's group is wheel on macOS, root on Linux). Leave out /opt/seamless/data when you are moving an existing install, whose data directory arrives there as a whole:

sudo install -d -o root -g wheel -m 0755 /opt/seamless /opt/seamless/bin /opt/seamless/etc
sudo install -d -o _seamless -g _seamless -m 0700 /opt/seamless/home /opt/seamless/data
sudo install -d -o _seamless -g _seamless -m 0755 /opt/seamless/run

A daemon that serves TLS keeps its certificate and key there too, out of your account's reach: the daemon's account cannot read a key in your home, and every process of yours can.

sudo install -d -o root -g _seamless -m 0750 /opt/seamless/etc/tls

Then pin the account: seam approve, seam touchid enroll, the Touch ID approver and serve accept only the account this file names as the daemon's, so no other account - a restricted one, another service's - can pass for it. sudo tee writes it as root's:

echo "_seamless $(id -u _seamless)" | sudo tee /opt/seamless/etc/daemon-account >/dev/null
sudo chmod 0644 /opt/seamless/etc/daemon-account

It is one line, the account's name and uid (_seamless 480). A pin that is not root's, that another account could rewrite (it or any directory above it), or that is not that one line makes them refuse every daemon until root rewrites it; seamlessd doctor says which.

The service runs as that account whether or not anyone is logged in. On macOS it is a LaunchDaemon: the plist, its controls, and how to retire the per-user service first are in the service reference. On Linux it is a system unit, /etc/systemd/system/seamless-daemon.service:

[Unit]
Description=Seamless daemon (peer_auth)
After=network.target

[Service]
User=_seamless
Group=_seamless
UMask=0077
Environment=SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml
Environment=HOME=/opt/seamless/home
ExecStart=/opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd serve
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now seamless-daemon

Retire any per-user service first, or it starts again at your next login (how).

Connect the owner

Your agents connect through the socket: a locked project opens only to a process the kernel names, which a TCP connection never is. Your config becomes a client's, because your account no longer runs the daemon - and a server-role config there would have seamlessd doctor report on a database in your home rather than the daemon's:

role: client
server_url: "unix:///opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock"

No key: the daemon names the caller by its uid. Then install the hooks and MCP registration:

seamlessd install-hooks --client claude    # or codex, or all

With a socket server_url every hook is a seam hook <event> command (Claude Code's own http hook cannot dial a socket), and the MCP registration is the seam mcp-proxy stdio bridge. They run the seam beside the seamlessd that installed them, a copy of your own; add --seam /opt/seamless/bin/seam to run the daemon's instead, which no process of yours can replace and which moves with the daemon when it updates itself. Under peer_auth the daemon reads no agent files, so seam hook reads them and sends what it found.

The console still needs TCP and the bearer key: a browser cannot dial a socket, and seamlessd console-open refuses a socket server_url with instructions. Keep the daemon's key in a second config of your own, used only for the console, and name it when you open the console:

# ~/.config/seamless/console.yaml, mode 0600
role: client
server_url: "http://127.0.0.1:8081"
mcp:
  api_key: "<the same key as the daemon's config>"

SEAMLESS_CONFIG=~/.config/seamless/console.yaml seamlessd console-open

On a daemon that locks a project, console-open signs in on the passkey origin the daemon names (which one) instead of 127.0.0.1: the console's cookie belongs to one host, and browsers refuse passkeys on an IP address. On a TLS install, server_url in console.yaml is the daemon's https address, as your other clients use it.

If your agents would write scripts over the data directory, tell them to use the tools or seam ... --json | jq instead: integrate your agent has the line to paste. Under peer_auth the directory is out of their reach either way.

Enroll an approver

An approver credential is what signs your approval: a passkey, or a Touch ID key. None is required: the terminal path below always works, and seamlessd doctor warns only that it is the one path left. Enrolling needs the daemon running under peer_auth, so do it after the cutover. A lock set from the console needs a passkey enrolled first.

Every credential needs a one-time enrollment code, and only the daemon's account can mint one; no route, over the socket or with the TCP key, can. A code works once, for 10 minutes, and only its hash is stored. It is minted for one key, named by its fingerprint, so a code someone else reads cannot enroll a different key. A passkey you already enrolled never vouches for a new one: an enrolled passkey can take a console lock off, so one touch you were tricked into must not be enough to add a key an agent holds. seamlessd approvers also lists credentials and removes them, and reset --yes drops every credential and revokes every live lease (reference).

Passkeys work with hardware keys, phones and password managers. Open /console/approvers on the passkey origin in your browser and create the passkey. The page then shows the command that mints a code for it:

sudo -k -u _seamless env SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml \
  /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd approvers enroll-code passkey --key XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX

Run it in your own terminal, check that the key it prints is the one on the page, and enter the code there. Browsers refuse passkeys on 127.0.0.1, so open the page on the passkey origin. Each passkey needs its own authenticator: the browser refuses one that already holds a passkey enrolled here, and devices that share synced passkeys, such as a phone on the same iCloud Keychain, count as one.

Touch ID on a Mac (optional) goes through Seamless Approve, a small macOS app that approves a request with Touch ID, an Apple Watch or the login password. A default install neither contains nor launches it, and Linux and Windows never see it. In your own terminal, with server_url naming the socket:

seam touchid enroll

It installs your seam's own release of the app (seamless-approve_<version>_darwin.zip, checked against the release's signed checksums.txt and against Apple's signature) at ~/Applications/Seamless Approve.app and opens it. Its window shows the new key's fingerprint and the command that mints a code for that key, to run in another terminal. Details, including how the app is checked and how a Mac re-enrolls, are in the CLI reference.

The app takes nothing from its command line but the socket and the request. It reads the request's facts and challenge from the daemon over the socket, refuses a socket served by your own account or by any account but the one the daemon names, and shows only the daemon's facts in the Touch ID prompt: the grant first, then the first three warnings. The agent's own reason is left out of that prompt on purpose. Its key is made in the Mac's Secure Enclave and kept in the data protection keychain under an access group only the signed app can claim, so another program running as you cannot sign with it, even behind a prompt of its own.

To build the app yourself you need macOS and Xcode's command-line tools. make approver-test runs its unit tests (no keychain, no prompt); make approver builds bin/approver/Seamless Approve.app, ad-hoc signed, and that build has no key store and says so. A usable build needs an Apple Developer account, an explicit macOS App ID com.arctop.seamless.approve, and a Developer ID provisioning profile for it whose keychain group covers the app's:

APPROVER_SIGN_IDENTITY=<identity hash> APPROVER_TEAM_ID=<team id> APPROVER_PROFILE=<file> make approver
seam touchid enroll --app "bin/approver/Seamless Approve.app"

scripts/approver/notarize.sh notarizes and staples a Developer ID build (APPROVER_NOTARY_KEY, APPROVER_NOTARY_KEY_ID, APPROVER_NOTARY_ISSUER_ID). A source or prerelease seam has no release of the app to fetch: pass --app with a downloaded zip or a local build.

The passkey origin

A passkey belongs to one relying party, named by its rp_id, and the browser creates or uses it only on that relying party's origins. Unless peer_auth.passkeys names them, the daemon picks:

  • A TLS install whose server_url names a host (a tailnet name, your own domain) uses that exact host as rp_id and https://<host>:<port> as the origin, the address your clients already use. Its parent domain is never used, so no other host under it can run a ceremony for these passkeys.
  • Any other install uses localhost and http://localhost:<port> (https with TLS on).

seamlessd doctor and the daemon's log at startup say which it is.

A passkey is bound to its rp_id for life. Changing rp_id, or the server_url it came from, or turning TLS off, strands every passkey enrolled under the old one. The daemon records each passkey's rp_id, so doctor and the log name the ones a change strands. Passkeys enrolled before it recorded that are listed as unknown.

A page on the origin can run passkey ceremonies with any passkey enrolled for it. That is why doctor checks two things about every origin:

  • The daemon listens on every address its host resolves to, on its port. A tailnet name can resolve to an IPv4 and an IPv6 address. An address of the name the daemon does not hold is one another process running as you can listen on and serve the same origin from, and a browser that picks that address runs its ceremonies there. So an IPv4 addr brings its interface's IPv6 addresses along: the tailnet's fd7a:... address beside its 100.x one, [::1] beside 127.0.0.1. Doctor's bind row lists them. It never pairs a private address with a global IPv6 one, which would widen a LAN bind to the internet. An address the pairing misses, such as one on another interface, still needs the wildcard (addr: "0.0.0.0:8081" holds every address of every interface, so the bearer key and TLS are then all that guard it on your LAN), or a name that resolves only to addresses the daemon holds.
  • The certificate names the host. Under peer_auth only root and the daemon's account read the TLS key, which is what keeps a process of yours from serving the origin with a valid certificate. That holds only if your account cannot get a certificate for the name by itself: a tailnet whose cert command you may run (tailscale cert) hands any process of yours one. Then binding every address is what stands between them and the origin.

Requests

When an agent reaches a locked project without a lease, Seamless files an access request, and the refusal says so. Asking needs no privilege, and the daemon, not the agent, supplies the facts you will see.

  • A call refused at the lock files one by itself, on the socket: a tool call that names the project, or that resolves its scope or session through a session recorded in it.
  • A session starting in the project's repository is recorded there, its name, cwd and model only, and the SessionStart hook files the request and answers with the locked notice instead of a briefing. The project's briefing arrives with the first Seamless tool result after the approval, once per lease, even across a daemon restart.
  • The agent can ask ahead, with the access_request tool (present only on a daemon that locks a project) or seam access request <project> --reason "..." from its own shell. The reason is at most 200 characters, and you see it quoted and labeled as the agent's own words.

access_request, and seam access request --json, answer with filed (true when this call filed a new request, false when it found one waiting or the agent already holds the access) and reason (added, kept or none). The rest of the behavior is the same for every path:

  • A request waits 15 minutes for your decision. One request waits per agent and project: asking again finds it, and an explicit reason fills in a waiting request's missing one.
  • After you deny one, the agent's next refused call says you denied it, and when, and files nothing: a refused call never asks you again behind your back. Its explicit request always files a new one, which is how it asks once you have told it what to ask for.
  • An agent that already holds the access it asks for is answered with it, and nothing is filed, until 30 minutes before it ends. From then on an explicit request files a refresh. A refresh carries the reason it was given; given none it shows "(no reason given)", and a later explicit reason fills that blank. Approving a refresh replaces the lease.

Requests name agents, not shells. A lease covers a process and everything it started, so a lease on a tmux server would open the project to every program in every pane, other agent sessions included. Seamless therefore files a request only for an agent: Claude Code, Codex, the Claude app's per-server wrapper, a process with one of those above it in the kernel-verified chain, or the JavaScript runtime a live session's hook stamped (Claude Code installed with npm runs as node). A process with no agent above it - seam run by hand in a tmux pane, a script from a login shell - is refused with the rule and this remedy: run the work from an agent session, which asks for itself. A shell, a multiplexer, a terminal or an editor that hosts terminals, a login process, the system's process manager, or any other application's own executable is never named by a request and never approved, on any path; deny one an older daemon filed. A session starting in a locked repository under such a process is not recorded at all.

What you are shown. Every approval surface shows the daemon's facts - the project, its isolation and the access asked for, the agent the daemon names, its pid and uid, the session and model, the working directory, whether this is a first request or a refresh, and until when it waits - with the agent's reason quoted and labeled as its own. Warnings come first, most serious first:

  1. the asking process is a broad process, on a request an older daemon filed (an approval will be refused);
  2. for a read grant, the project's content may be copied into the asking project's memories;
  3. the session read text from outside (a web page, a file it was handed), so its reason may not be its own;
  4. the same agent is also asking for another project;
  5. the session works outside the project's repository;
  6. no session names the agent, so its cwd and model are unknown;
  7. the agent already holds a lease on the project, and approving replaces it.

The facts carry a digest. When any of them changes before you decide (a reason filled in, a new mark on the session, another request from the same agent), the approval is refused and you look again.

Approve: three paths, one core

Every path ends in the same check: the facts you saw still hold, the proof is valid, and the lease is written once, bound to the request. Answering a dialog is never the approval, because any process of your account, or a client hook, could answer one.

Path The proof Where
The dialog in the agent's session Touch ID, or a passkey on the request's page the agent's client, on the socket
seam approve sudo -k to the daemon's account, every time your own terminal
The passkey page a passkey the request's console page, in your browser

The dialog. When the agent's client declared MCP elicitation on the socket and a proof can finish in the dialog, a refused call (or access_request) shows you the request's facts, warnings first, in the client itself: Claude Code shows it, and so do Codex builds that declare form elicitation. You choose a duration and Touch ID or a passkey. Touch ID runs the Seamless Approve app, which reads the facts from the daemon and signs over the request, the facts' digest, the access and the duration. A passkey opens the request's page for the duration you chose, and it signs the duration and the facts' digest too, so a tampered duration fails verification. Where a passkey is the only way the dialog can finish, the dialog is that page.

The call waits up to 110 seconds from its start, then answers with the request still pending for the paths below. Declining or dismissing denies nothing, and an agent's connection cannot deny at all: the request waits for you. Cancelling the Touch ID prompt, or the helper closing or being killed after it was seen, ends the wait at once, the request still pending. There is at most one dialog per request per connection, and it survives a daemon restart: the daemon keeps a connection's declared dialog modes, for clients on the socket only and only while a lock or read grants are configured, until the connection has gone unused for 30 days. An agent connected before the release that keeps them shows the plain refusal until its next initialize.

seam approve. In your own terminal (it refuses without one, so an agent cannot use it), seam approve lists what is waiting and shows the facts, asks for a duration, and commits the decision with sudo -k -u <daemon account> seamlessd approve. The sudo -k asks for your Touch ID or password every time, and becoming the daemon's account is the proof. Typing deny in full at the duration question, or d at the confirmation, denies. seam approve --watch prints each new request and raises a notification. Every flag and message is in the CLI reference.

The passkey page. /console/access/<id> shows the request's facts; choose a duration and sign with an enrolled passkey (seam approve --passkey opens it, and --for chooses the duration, which the page then shows read-only). The page denies without a passkey. /console/access lists every waiting request, every live lease with Revoke, and every console unlock with Lock again.

Which paths a refusal offers, and when. Every remedy offers only the paths this daemon has for this call:

Path Offered when
seam approve <id> in your terminal always
Touch ID in the approval dialog a Touch ID key is enrolled, and the client declared form elicitation on the socket. The SessionStart notice runs before MCP connects, so it offers Touch ID to Claude Code, and to Codex with "if this Codex shows one"
A passkey at the request's page passkeys are set up and at least one is enrolled

A call over the TCP key, whose bearer key can never hold a lease, is told to work from an agent session on the socket instead, and no request is filed. Once a dialog ends with the request still pending, the remedy says how it ended and which paths are left.

The durations are: until the session ends (the default, at most peer_auth.max_lease), 1 hour, or 4 hours, each capped by max_lease.

Leases and the process tree

An approval is a lease on one agent process. It covers that process and every process it started: the MCP bridge, seam commands, the hooks and the agent's own scripts share one approval, and nothing outside the tree does.

The daemon learns the tree from the kernel alone. At accept it reads which process holds the socket connection (the audit token on macOS, which names the last process to use it, and SO_PEERCRED and a pidfd on Linux) and pins that pid to the process, so a later walk can tell it from one that reused the pid. Per request it walks the parent chain from there, verifying every link. A link that does not verify ends the chain, so an orphan reparented to init, or a reused pid, reaches nothing above it. Nothing the client sends, the self-reported agent-process header included, enters the chain. Only the owner's socket connections can hold a lease; a TCP request never can.

A lease ends at its expiry, when its session ends (session_end, or the client's own session-end hook), when you Revoke it on /console/access, when you run seamlessd approvers reset --yes, or when the database is restored from a snapshot (a rollback or seamlessd import). Nothing extends one silently. From 30 minutes before it ends, every tool result and hook injection says when it ends and how to ask again.

A console unlock is separate. A browser opens a locked project from its unlock page, /console/unlock/<project>, for at most three hours (less when max_lease is shorter), in one of two ways. Unlock with a passkey asks your authenticator there. Approve from a terminal shows a code and the command that approves it, for example:

sudo -k -u _seamless seamlessd console-open --unlock example-finance --code 7KQ2-M9XD

Run it in your own terminal. sudo -k asks for your password or Touch ID, and the page updates by itself once the code is approved. The unlock opens the browser that showed the code and no other, so the code is not a secret: reading it off your screen or terminal gives nothing away. A code works once, within ten minutes, and --for 1h makes the unlock shorter. Approve only a code your own browser shows: one you were handed would unlock someone else's browser.

Either way the unlock lives in that one browser, never as a lease, and it never opens the project to an agent. It is a cookie plus a key that the browser keeps for the console's own address. A browser sends its cookies to every port of the same host, so the cookie alone opens nothing. Before an unlock begins, the page creates the key and installs a small service worker that signs each console request with it. The browser lets only the console's own address use the key, and the daemon counts the unlock only on a request the key signed. A browser that cannot run the service worker can't hold an unlock, and the page says so. That covers some private windows, and any page that is neither https nor localhost. A locked plan or session page in the console takes you to that unlock page.

Read grants and the advisory tier

Read grants (isolation.requests: true) turn a read refused at a confidential project's fence into a request. A grant is read-only, one project, for a limited time, and never involves a sealed project on either side.

Under peer_auth a grant is bound to the asking agent's process tree, as a lease is, and takes the same proofs: seam approve, a passkey or a Touch ID key. Without peer_auth the approval is advisory. seam approve asks for a y/N in a terminal and commits over the console with the bearer key, and the console's Approve does the same, so any process that holds the key can approve a request, its own included. The holder of an advisory grant is also the session a call speaks for, which is self-reported: an agent that rebinds with session_start, or names another session with session=, writes where that session may, past the grant's write confinement. Under peer_auth the holder is the process tree, and the same moves are refused. Use the advisory tier to keep an agent from wandering into a confidential project, not against one set on it.

Neither tier stops an agent running as you from reading a confidential or sealed project. A session's project is the agent's word, so session_start project=<slug>, a hook naming that repository, or session= on a tool reads the project with no grant at all, and the console answers your account for every project that is not locked. The fence keeps a careful agent out. The lock holds against one set on it, because it asks the kernel who is calling, so lock a project that must stay shut. A restricted account has none of these ways in.

A grant's write confinement binds the asking agent's process tree. A process that detaches from that tree, or a call over TCP with the bearer key, is not confined.

A2A speaks for no session, so under peer_auth it refuses a confidential or sealed project unless the caller holds a lease on it.

Restricted local accounts

A restricted local account is a second OS account on the machine whose agents work beside yours: a separate login for unattended agents, say, so that nothing they run can read your home directory. With the daemon's account pinned, it may be any account other than the daemon's; without the pin it must be an ordinary account, the kind a person logs in with, since the clients then accept any system account as the daemon's. List it under peer_auth.restricted, by user name or numeric uid:

peer_auth:
  enabled: true
  owner: alice
  socket:
    path: /opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock
  force_locked: [example-finance]
  restricted: [_example_agent]

What such an account reaches:

  • Every open project that is not locked, reading and writing. A project whose isolation is confidential or sealed, and every locked project, is out of its reach and is not listed for it. Its refusal reads the same for those projects and for a slug nobody registered, so it never learns which closed projects exist.

  • The global scope, read-only. Its briefing, recall and reads include global memories and notes; every global write is refused.

  • No new projects. A write or a session naming a project that does not exist is refused rather than creating it. You create the projects and map the account's clones of your repositories to them, as the daemon's account:

    sudo -u _seamless env SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml \
  /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd map-repo --path /Users/_example_agent/repos/example-app --project example-app

    A session started anywhere else - an unmapped directory, a closed project's repository - is not recorded.

  • No approvals. It files no access requests, gets no read grants and holds no leases, so nothing it does can open a locked or confidential project.

It is known only through the socket. The kernel names it by its uid, exactly as it names you; it never holds the bearer key, and a TCP request is always yours. Its config lives in its own home (~/.config/seamless/seamless.yaml, mode 0600):

role: client
server_url: "unix:///opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock"

No key. Then install its hooks and MCP bridge as the account, and run the session as the account (sudo -u _example_agent -H claude). The account needs its own Claude Code sign-in and its own copy of anything the session reads:

sudo -u _example_agent -H /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd install-hooks --client claude \
  --seam /opt/seamless/bin/seam

Keep the socket outside every home directory: the account cannot traverse yours.

Everything it writes is labeled. Memories, notes, tasks and its rewrites of yours, plan steps, sessions and their findings, and trials record the account that wrote them, and every surface shows it: "[written by account _example_agent]" at the end of briefing, prompt recall (<seam-recall>), A2A and seam task list lines, an account field in tool results, and a "written by account _example_agent" chip on console rows. Your own writes look exactly as they always have. A label stays while the account's words may still be there. A status change, a claim or release, tags or a star never move it, and neither does your append, partial edit or rewrite of one field. It clears once you have rewritten all of the item's text in new words: a memory's body and description, a note's body, title and description, or a task's title and body. An empty description or task body counts as yours.

Binding rules are proposals. A constraint, convention, protocol or stage steers every session's briefing, so one from a restricted account does not land on its own. When the account writes one, or edits, appends to, supersedes, overwrites or deletes one (yours or its own), the write waits on the console's Held screen as a proposal, "proposed by account _example_agent", and nothing in the corpus changes. It is in no briefing or recall, the account's own included, until you promote it:

seam proposals              # pending proposals, newest first
seam promote <id>           # land it as written, labeled with the account
seam proposals discard <id> # drop it

Promoting is yours alone, on the console or in your terminal; the account can neither promote a proposal nor undo a promotion. Every other kind of memory, and notes, tasks and findings, lands at once, labeled.

Three more rules keep its text from passing as yours. It cannot give a project memory the name of a live global constraint, convention, protocol or stage, because a read by that name would then answer with its text. A project memory it wrote before you created a global rule of that name does not answer either: a read by the bare name answers with your rule and names the account's memory, which stays readable by id or with project=<slug>. A write by that bare name (an append, edit, delete, star or supersede) is refused until it says project=<slug> or project=global. It cannot ask the gardener to plan a change (gardener_request, gardener_split), and it still sees proposals with gardener_proposals. A memory or note whose content it changes loses its star.

Sessions belong to the account that started them: a restricted account's agents cannot resume, bind to or write findings into your sessions, and yours cannot act in theirs. Its sessions also have names of their own: every one is stored as _example_agent:<name> (_example_agent:cc/... for its Claude Code sessions), and every session name its agents give is read inside that namespace. A name you already use, in any project, is simply free for it, so the account cannot learn which session names exist where it cannot look. The console and seam show its sessions by the qualified name, and that is the name you use for them. You cannot start a session of your own under a name beginning _example_agent:.

Verify

# As root or the daemon's account: the policy, and nothing serve would refuse.
sudo -u _seamless env SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd doctor

# As the owner: the files are out of reach, and the lock holds.
ls /opt/seamless/data                               # Permission denied
seam recall something --project example-finance     # refused at the lock

# As any other account: refused at the door.
curl --unix-socket /opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock http://localhost/healthz   # 403

Then start an agent in the locked project's repository: its session starts with the locked notice, and seam approve in your own terminal shows its request.

What changes with peer_auth on

  • The daemon reads no agent files; your hooks do. Under peer_auth every path a hook names was chosen by another account, and the daemon can read its own data directory, so it opens none of them. When server_url names the peer_auth socket, seam hook (running as you, beside the agent) reads the transcript, the plan file and the subagent transcript itself and sends what it found: session-end findings and token totals, the model, plan and subagent capture, and the git head. The daemon treats this as your agent's claim and applies the usual rules: in a locked project it lands only once you approve a lease for that agent. Until then the hook says in one line on stderr (and, for a plan, in the agent's context) that the capture was not recorded; nothing is retried, and the next capture after the approval carries the current state. Agents on the TCP key make none of these captures; point their server_url at the socket. Agents can still record findings with session_end.
  • Updates are yours to switch on. The installer's per-user service cannot host peer_auth, so neither the installer nor a seamlessd update run as you touches this install, and by default the daemon only tells you about a new release: replace /opt/seamless/bin with sudo and restart it. It can also update itself. Run make install only with a client-role config, so it updates your own seam and hooks and leaves the service alone.
  • Counts stay machine-wide in usage_summary, as they are for isolation: volume, never content, and the same number for every caller.
  • The gardener still runs over every project, as the daemon, for no caller. Its proposals about a locked project reach a client only through a lease, and the console shows them only in a browser that has unlocked the project.

Updates

A peer_auth daemon can install new releases by itself, with no installer and no root process, once an administrator opts it in:

  1. Give the daemon's account the binary directory: sudo chown -R _seamless:_seamless /opt/seamless/bin.
  2. Set update.auto: true in its config, /opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml. Only root writes that file, so without that line the console's toggle cannot switch automatic updates on here; with it, the toggle can still turn them off.
  3. On Linux, let the account's systemd user manager run with no one logged in: sudo loginctl enable-linger _seamless. The updater runs as a unit of that manager, because stopping the system unit stops every process in it.
  4. Restart the daemon. Settings -> Updates (its Mode row) then reads "installs new releases by itself", or names the step still missing.

The service must start the daemon again after a clean exit, as the plist and the unit above do (KeepAlive true, Restart=always); Restart=on-failure would leave it down after an update. On Linux, keep every setting in the config file: a SEAMLESS_* variable on an Environment= line of the unit, other than SEAMLESS_CONFIG, never reaches the updater, so it makes the daemon only notify.

From then on the usual rules hold: the soak, the quiet moment, the backup, the confirmation and the rollback. Only the install step differs. Running as the daemon's account, the updater verifies the release's checksums.txt against its Sigstore bundle for the exact tag, checks the archive against it, keeps the seamlessd and seam it replaces beside the new ones, renames the new ones into place, and ends the daemon with SIGTERM. launchd's KeepAlive or systemd's Restart=always then starts the new binary. A rollback renames the kept ones back the same way. Hooks installed with --seam /opt/seamless/bin/seam (Connect the owner) move with the daemon. To update by hand:

sudo -u _seamless /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd update --config /opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml

The trade-off: the daemon's account can now rewrite its own binary, so a compromised daemon could keep itself in place across restarts. It already holds every project's data, and your account still cannot write either binary, so the boundary against your agents is unchanged.

Limits

  • The transcript holds what a session read. Once you approve an agent, its project's content is in that session's transcript and any tool result it kept. A lease ending does not unread it.
  • An approval is only as strong as its proof. seam approve proves itself only through sudo -k, so a passwordless or seamlessd-only sudoers rule voids it. seam approve warns when sudo -n shows it needs no authentication, which a rule scoped to seamlessd alone does not trigger. Touch ID and passkeys are as strong as your device and the user verification they require.
  • A debugger running as you can act inside an approval. It can attach to any process in the agent's tree. macOS limits this with the hardened runtime and SIP, and Linux with yama's ptrace_scope (1 or higher); neither stops root.
  • The boundary is the OS account. Root, and anyone who can become the daemon's account, reads everything; a passwordless sudo to it voids the whole arrangement. Whoever holds the bearer key acts as the owner, and reaches every project but the locked ones. Backups of the data directory, and exports, hold every project: keep them as carefully as the most sensitive project in them. An export records the locks, and importing one checks for a passkey that can open them.
  • Anything running as you can watch your terminal. A tmux server your agents share lets them capture the pane, and your clipboard is reachable too. Nothing the approval commands show is a credential: a console unlock's code opens only the browser that showed it, and an enrollment code enrolls only the key it was minted for, so being read gives neither away. Check that the code you approve is the one your browser shows, and that the key the enrollment command prints is the one on your screen.
  • An unlocked browser shows the project to whatever controls that browser. A program running as you can receive the console's cookies by opening your browser on another port, but without the browser's key they open nothing. What it can still do is drive the browser itself, capture your screen, or read the browser's profile files, which hold the key. Safari wraps the key with one in your keychain; other browsers may store it as is. Lock the project again on the access page once you are done, rather than wait out the three hours.
  • Taking a lock off is one passkey touch, and it holds for every agent. Removing a lock set from the console takes a single passkey approval, and from the restart that follows every agent of yours reaches the project as its isolation allows, with no approval, until you lock it again. A project listed under peer_auth.force_locked keeps its lock: the console cannot take it off, even with a passkey, though a console unlock still opens it in one browser for a while.
  • Your shell is yours to guard. Under peer_auth seam approve works only over the socket, and refuses one that the daemon's account does not serve, so a changed server_url cannot show it false facts. An agent running as you can still edit your shell's startup files, or replace a seam you own. Run /opt/seamless/bin/seam approve, which your account cannot write, by its full path if you doubt yours.
  • Some decisions refuse a process an agent started: bringing a fence down, releasing or discarding a held write, clearing a session's mark, and changing which features are on. Make them in your own terminal or the console. This stops an agent's ordinary tool calls, not one that detaches a process from its tree or reads the key in your console.yaml.

Move an existing install over

The data directory moves as a whole; the database stores paths relative to it, so nothing inside needs rewriting. On one volume the move is a rename.

  1. Fence first, in the old world. Make each project you will lock confidential or sealed (seam project isolation <slug> confidential --yes).

  2. Back up, as the owner, while the old daemon still serves: seamlessd export -o ~/seamless-before-peer-auth.tar.gz. The archive holds every project, the locked ones included: keep it as carefully as they are.

  3. Create the account, the layout and the pin above, leaving out /opt/seamless/data, and install root-owned copies of both binaries in /opt/seamless/bin (sudo install -o root -m 0755 <seamlessd> <seam> /opt/seamless/bin/). Keep a copy of the current mcp.api_key for the console.

  4. Write the daemon's config at /opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml (root:_seamless 0640): your old config with data_dir: /opt/seamless/data, the peer_auth block listing the projects to lock, and the same mcp.api_key and LLM keys. Check the slugs against your project list now: a misspelled entry is refused at startup, and doctor names it.

    If the daemon serves TLS, its certificate and key move too: the old config points into your home, which the daemon's account cannot read and every process of yours can. Copy them into /opt/seamless/etc/tls (sudo install -o root -g _seamless -m 0644 <cert> /opt/seamless/etc/tls/ and sudo install -o root -g _seamless -m 0640 <key> /opt/seamless/etc/tls/), point tls.cert_file and tls.key_file at those copies, and delete the key from your home once the new daemon serves. Whatever renews the certificate (tailscale cert, certbot) must from then on write there, as root: serve refuses a key another account can read, and doctor names the file.

  5. Stop the old service and move the data: stop and remove the per-user service (how), then sudo mv ~/.seamless /opt/seamless/data, sudo chown -R _seamless:_seamless /opt/seamless/data and sudo chmod -R go-rwx /opt/seamless/data.

  6. Start the daemon: install and load the LaunchDaemon or the system unit above, then curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/healthz and the doctor line in Verify.

  7. Switch your own config to the socket and reinstall the hooks and MCP registration (Connect the owner). This is the step that puts your agents on seam mcp-proxy.

  8. Enroll an approver (how). Until you do, the terminal path still approves.

  9. Verify (above), then start an agent in a locked repository and approve its request end to end.

  10. Put the export out of your agents' reach. The archive from step 2 sits in your home, readable by anything that runs as you, with every locked project in it. Move it now (sudo mv ~/seamless-before-peer-auth.tar.gz /opt/seamless/ and sudo chown root and sudo chmod 600 the file there), and delete it once the new install has proved itself.

  11. Optional: list a restricted account. Add it to peer_auth.restricted and restart the daemon. Give the account its own client config (socket server_url, no key), run install-hooks as the account, and map each of its clones with seamlessd map-repo --path <its clone> --project <slug> as the daemon's account (details).

Roll back

Unload the LaunchDaemon or disable the system unit (how), move the data back (sudo mv /opt/seamless/data ~/.seamless and sudo chown -R $(id -un) ~/.seamless), restore your server config without the peer_auth block - a release that predates it refuses the key - and reinstall the per-user service (make install, or the installer). A TLS key you deleted from your home in step 4 comes back the same way (sudo install -o $(id -un) -m 0600 /opt/seamless/etc/tls/<key> <the old path>), or the per-user daemon cannot load its certificate. The export from step 2, wherever step 10 put it, is the fallback if anything in the move went wrong.
